summary: Defines Traversal Using Relays around NAT, a protocol that lets a host behind a NAT use a relay server to exchange packets with peers when direct communication is impossible. A client can talk to multiple peers using a single relay address. It was designed as part of the Interactive Connectivity Establishment approach. It replaces RFC 5766.

eli5.summary: If two kids cannot reach each other across a fence, they can pass notes through a helper standing at a gate. TURN is the helper for computers stuck behind a home router.

subtitle: How a host stuck behind a NAT borrows a public relay server to swap packets with its peers.

tldr.problem: Two hosts behind badly behaved NATs often cannot reach each other directly, even with hole punching, and some firewalls block direct UDP altogether.
tldr.mechanism: A client asks a TURN server for an allocation, a public relayed transport address. Peers send to that address, and the server forwards their data to the client inside TURN messages that say which peer sent it. The client sends data the same way in reverse.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8656 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5766 and RFC 6156. It adds IPv6 and DTLS support, among other changes.

today: RFC 8656 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It obsoletes RFC 5766 and RFC 6156, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Relay Is Needed
sections.content:
A host behind a NAT often wants to exchange packets with other hosts, some of them also behind NATs. Hosts first try hole punching to find a direct path. The RFC notes that this generally fails when both sides sit behind NATs with address-dependent or address- and port-dependent mapping.

When no direct path exists, an intermediate host has to relay the packets. TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) is the protocol a client uses to control such a relay and to exchange packets with its peers through it. Its distinguishing feature is that one relay address can serve several peers at once.

Relaying has a cost: the server typically needs a high-bandwidth Internet connection. The RFC therefore says to use TURN only when a direct path cannot be found. TURN was designed as one piece of the ICE approach to NAT traversal, which searches for a direct path first, but it can be used without ICE. It is an extension of STUN, and most TURN messages are STUN-formatted.

The RFC names other reasons to relay too: enterprise firewalls that block direct UDP but allow relayed UDP, and users who want IP location privacy from the remote peer.
sections.eli5: Sometimes two computers cannot find a way to talk straight to each other. TURN lets them both talk to a helper in the middle, who passes everything along. It costs the helper effort, so it is the last resort.

sections.title: Clients, Peers and Relayed Addresses
sections.content:
The TURN client is the host behind the NAT. The TURN server sits on the public Internet. A peer is a host the client wants to reach; peers do not speak TURN. The server hands the client a relayed transport address, an IP address and port on the server. When a peer sends a packet there, the server relays the data to the client.

Everything revolves around the allocation: the relayed transport address plus its state, such as permissions and expiry timers. The client and server both identify an allocation by the 5-tuple of client address and port, server address and port, and transport protocol. A client that wants a second relayed address must use a different 5-tuple.

Between client and server, TURN messages can travel over UDP, TCP, TLS over TCP, or DTLS over UDP. Between server and peer, this specification always uses UDP. TCP is supported because some firewalls block UDP entirely. The server converts between the two transports when it relays.

When a peer is behind a NAT, the client must name it by its server-reflexive transport address (the address on the outside of the NAT), not its host address. How the client and peers learn each other's addresses is out of scope; ICE or a rendezvous protocol such as SIP can carry them.

TURN servers are designed to run as ordinary user-space applications. The RFC lists the consequences: Diffserv and ECN values may not be preserved, the TTL may be reset rather than decremented, and there is no end-to-end fragmentation because the server reassembles packets.
sections.eli5: The helper gives you a mailbox of your own at the gate. Anyone who drops a note in that mailbox, the helper carries to you, and the note says who sent it.

sections.title: Allocations, Refreshes and Permissions
sections.content:
The client creates an allocation with an Allocate request. The server requires authentication (the mandatory-to-implement mechanism is the STUN long-term credential mechanism), so the usual first try gets a 401 error and the second, with credentials, succeeds. The success response carries the relayed transport address.

An allocation has a default lifetime of 10 minutes (600 seconds). The client keeps it alive with Refresh requests, and may ask for a different lifetime. Sending data to a peer does not refresh an allocation. A Refresh with a requested lifetime of zero deletes it. TURN uses Refresh rather than a repeated Allocate so the client learns if the allocation has vanished.

Permissions limit who can use the relay. A permission is an IP address and a lifetime. The server relays an incoming datagram only if its source IP address matches a permission and silently discards it otherwise. Permissions expire after 5 minutes unless refreshed and cannot be deleted. A client installs or refreshes them with CreatePermission (several at once is allowed) or ChannelBind, and only authenticated transactions can do this.

The RFC also covers a dual-stack client trying a TURN server over IPv4 and IPv6 in the manner of Happy Eyeballs, the EVEN-PORT attribute for older RTP that wants an even port with the next port reserved, and packet translation between IPv4 and IPv6 on the server.
sections.eli5: You rent the mailbox for a short time and must keep telling the helper you still want it. You also give the helper a list of names allowed to leave notes, and that list expires too.

sections.title: Sending Data: Send, Data and Channels
sections.content:
TURN has two ways to move application data. The first uses Send indications (client to server) and Data indications (server to client). Each carries an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS attribute naming the peer and a DATA attribute holding the payload. The client must install a permission for the peer first. Indications cannot be authenticated, so applications that want end-to-end security should encrypt data between client and peer.

The second way uses channels. A Send or Data indication adds 36 bytes of overhead, which can hurt VoIP bandwidth. The client sends a ChannelBind request that ties a channel number to a peer's transport address. After that, data travels in compact ChannelData messages with a 4-byte header. A binding lasts 10 minutes unless refreshed, cannot be deleted, and the client must wait 5 minutes after expiry before reusing the number or address differently.

A client can mix both: bind a channel for busy peers and use indications for others. Once a channel is bound the server always uses ChannelData towards the client. Valid channel numbers run from 0x4000 through 0x4FFF, 4096 values. Numbers below that conflict with the STUN header, and 0x5000 through 0xFFFF are reserved for DTLS-SRTP multiplexing collision avoidance.

The RFC also advises avoiding IP fragmentation. Applications should assume a path MTU of 1280 bytes, and about 500 bytes of application data per message will generally avoid fragmentation. The DONT-FRAGMENT attribute lets a client ask the server to set the DF bit towards the peer.
sections.eli5: At first every note goes in a big envelope with a long label. If you chat a lot with one friend, you agree on a short nickname, a channel number, so the envelopes are much smaller.

sections.title: The ChannelData Message and STUN Codes
sections.content:
Unlike other TURN messages, ChannelData does not use the STUN header. It has a 2-byte Channel Number, a 2-byte Length counting only the application data (zero is valid), and then the application data. Because ChannelData shares a port with other protocols, a receiver can tell it apart by its first byte: values 64 to 79 mean a TURN channel, while 0 to 3 mean STUN.

The other TURN messages are STUN methods: Allocate (0x003), Refresh (0x004), Send (0x006), Data (0x007), CreatePermission (0x008) and ChannelBind (0x009). This document also defines attributes such as LIFETIME, XOR-PEER-ADDRESS, XOR-RELAYED-ADDRESS, DATA, REQUESTED-TRANSPORT and RESERVATION-TOKEN. REQUESTED-TRANSPORT only allows code point 17, UDP.

New error codes include 403 (Forbidden), 437 (Allocation Mismatch), 441 (Wrong Credentials), 442 (Unsupported Transport Protocol), 486 (Allocation Quota Reached) and 508 (Insufficient Capacity). Codes 440 and 443 handle address family problems.
sections.eli5: A normal TURN message is a letter with a full address block. A ChannelData message is a tiny tag that says only the nickname and the length, followed by what you want to say.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most attacks are blocked by requiring authentication, so the RFC requires it. The mandatory mechanism is STUN's long-term credential mechanism, which stops outsiders from obtaining allocations or faking refreshes and permissions. It is open to offline dictionary attacks on low-entropy passwords. Strong passwords help, and (D)TLS between client and server mitigates the risk further.

Because Send and Data indications are not authenticated, an attacker can inject bogus Send indications. Requiring a permission for the peer partly mitigates this.

Two loop attacks are described. In the TURN loop attack, an attacker uses spoofed addresses and channel bindings to make a packet bounce between two TURN servers. Mitigations include authenticated requests, randomized relay ports, per-username bandwidth limits and decrementing the TTL. In the tunnel amplification attack, a packet bounces between a TURN server and an IPv4/IPv6 tunnel. The RFC states that servers MUST NOT accept Teredo or 6to4 addresses in allocation or channel-binding requests.

The permission system exists to reassure enterprise administrators that TURN cannot simply bypass firewall security.
sections.eli5: The helper only works for people who show a password. Without that, strangers could use the helper to hide who they are or trick it into passing a note around in circles.

sections.title: Changes From Earlier TURN RFCs
sections.content:
TURN was first published as RFC 5766, and RFC 6156 later added IPv6 support. RFC 8656 obsoletes both.

The changes since RFC 5766 include IPv6 support, the REQUESTED-ADDRESS-FAMILY attribute, DTLS support, receiving ICMP packets, updated path MTU discovery guidance, discovery of TURN servers, TURN URI scheme semantics, Happy Eyeballs for TURN, and alignment with RFC 8489 (STUN). The document also describes the tunnel amplification attack.

Relative to RFC 6156 it adds the ADDITIONAL-ADDRESS-FAMILY and ADDRESS-ERROR-CODE attributes, new 440 and 443 responses, more detail on packet translation, and TCP-to-UDP and UDP-to-TCP relaying.

One compatibility warning: the channel number range is not backwards compatible with RFC 5766, so a client following the older RFC might fail to bind channels on a server following this one.
sections.eli5: This is the updated rulebook. It folds two older rulebooks together and adds new rules for newer kinds of addresses and safer connections.

messages.label: Allocate success
messages.note: Carries the relayed address, 192.0.2.15:50000 in the RFC's example.

messages.label: Refresh request
messages.note: Sent some time later to keep the allocation.

fields.name: Channel Number
fields.desc: Identifies the channel and thus the peer; allowed values are 0x4000 through 0x4FFF.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the application data that follows; zero is valid.

items.label: Refresh
items.desc: Request/response only. Extends or deletes an allocation.

items.label: Send
items.desc: Indication only. Client sends data to a peer.

items.label: Data
items.desc: Indication only. Server delivers a peer's data to the client.

items.label: CreatePermission
items.desc: Request/response only. Installs or refreshes permissions.

items.label: ChannelBind
items.desc: Request/response only. Binds a channel number to a peer.
